Formulation:
- Predisposing factors: Female patient with prior brief similar episode approximately one month ago.
- Precipitating factors: Sudden onset of continuous rotational vertigo ~2 hours prior while standing (making breakfast).
- Perpetuating factors: Ongoing vertigo, nausea, unsteadiness and tinnitus preventing normal ambulation; formal ear/neurological examination and vitals not yet performed.
- Protective factors: Immediate clinical contact, prescription issued, plan for GP review/ear examination, presence of spouse.
- Integration with DDx: Clinical presentation consistent with acute peripheral vestibular disorder (vestibular neuritis or labyrinthitis) per DDx; clinician labeled labyrinthitis. Central causes (posterior circulation stroke/TIA) less likely clinically given absence of focal neurological signs reported, but not excluded without formal examination/imaging.

Mental Health Care Plan Details

Principal Problem: Acute vertigo with nausea and tinnitus (clinician diagnosis: labyrinthitis; DDx: vestibular neuritis likely)
- Patient Goal(s): Symptom relief (reduce vertigo/nausea), be able to walk safely, obtain GP/ear examination and follow-up.
- Clinical Goal(s): Symptomatic control of vertigo and nausea; perform focused ear and neurological examination and vital signs; exclude central causes if indicated; arrange further ENT/neurology assessment if symptoms persist or hearing loss develops.
- Actions (Patient):
  - Take prescribed medication as issued (medication name not documented; instructions recorded as one tablet three times daily for ~10 days).
  - Contact support to book GP appointment for ear and neurological examination (patient agreed to book).
  - Seek immediate emergency care (A&E) if developing new limb weakness, sudden severe headache, becoming violently sick, or other rapid deterioration (advice given in transcript).
- Actions (Clinician/GP):
  - Review patient in person to examine ears (otoscopy), assess gait and cranial nerve/neurological function, and check blood pressure and other vitals (as recommended in transcript).
  - Consider ENT referral if examination suggests inner ear pathology or persistent symptoms/hearing changes.
  - Consider urgent imaging (CT/MRI) or stroke pathway if focal neurological signs or vascular risk factors present on exam.
  - Provide symptomatic treatments (antiemetic/vestibular suppressants) as clinically indicated — prescription already issued per transcript (medication name not documented). Document medication name and dosing clearly at in-person review.

Secondary Problem (if applicable):
- Not recorded / Not applicable

Patient Education, Emergency Care & Relapse Prevention:
- Education Given: Yes. Topics Covered: clinician diagnosis (labyrinthitis explained), purpose of symptomatic medication, need for GP review/ear examination, and explicit warning signs requiring immediate A&E attendance (new limb weakness, sudden severe headache, violent vomiting).
- Early Warning Signs of Relapse/Worsening: New focal neurological deficits (weakness), sudden severe headache, severe uncontrollable vomiting, progressive worsening of gait/coordination.
- Coping Strategies: Not recorded beyond advice to take prescribed medication and seek medical review; resting and avoiding activities that risk falls implied by advice to seek assessment before resuming normal activities (not explicitly recorded).

- Review Date: Not recorded; plan documented to have in-person GP review "in the next few days" (patient advised to book appointment).

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)
- Vestibular neuritis — Likelihood: High. Justification: Sudden onset continuous rotational vertigo with nausea and imbalance without reported hearing loss — DDx favored vestibular neuritis as most consistent.
- Labyrinthitis — Likelihood: Medium. Justification: Tinnitus reported and acute vertigo/nausea are compatible with inner ear inflammation; clinician diagnosed labyrinthitis in the transcript.
- Vestibular migraine — Likelihood: Medium. Justification: Recurrent vertiginous episode history (prior brief episode) and vertigo without clear hearing loss can be consistent with vestibular migraine; no migraine history documented.

Quality checks
● Missing but clinically expected elements: vital signs (blood pressure, pulse), focused neurological/cranial nerve exam findings, formal ear examination/otoscopy findings, medication name and exact dose/route, full DOB (day/month), formal MSE, explicit suicide/self-harm risk assessment, documented follow-up appointment date/time, and hearing assessment results.
● Internal conflicts between transcript and DDx: clinician diagnosed labyrinthitis while DDx reasoning ranks vestibular neuritis as most likely — conflict noted.
● Transcript quality notes: some phrases unclear or truncated (clinician speech includes occasional mis-transcription e.g., "charting premature hearing failure" vs patient statement of premature ovarian failure); medication name omitted in transcript; clinician noted limited visibility of patient's face on video; overall dialogue contains brief pauses and incomplete lines.
